title: Infection: why being ill feels the way it does
description: When the body fights an infection such as flu, the tiredness, slowness, low mood and loss of interest are not just side effects. They are produced by the brain in response to signals from the immune system. The episode follows what has been measured in healthy volunteers given a vaccine or a small dose of a bacterial substance that sets off a mild, safe immune response. There is no "typical response" to compare with: this is the typical response.
caveat: These studies use a mild immune challenge in healthy volunteers and scan them about two hours later. That is a stand-in for a real infection. In the vaccine study body temperature did not rise, while in the endotoxin study it did. Fever is part of the same brain-directed response; in rodents it is set off in a small area of the hypothalamus, the median preoptic nucleus, which is too small to draw here, so nothing is drawn for fever. Most findings come from two small groups of volunteers, sixteen men in one and thirty-nine people in the other, and several were seen only while people did a particular task in the scanner. A pooled analysis confirms that inflammation goes with changes in these regions, without regard to their direction. How the brain recovers as the infection clears was not studied.

phases.name: The alarm is raised
phases.caption: Immune cells meet the infection and release signalling molecules that act on the brain. The brain then produces the sickness response: fever, sleepiness, loss of appetite, aching. No brain region is drawn changing yet, because the sources read do not say where this first step happens in people.

phases.name: Tired and slowed
phases.timescale: two to three hours in the studies
phases.caption: Tiredness, fogginess and slower reactions set in. Regions that represent the state of the body, including the insula, become more active, and activity changes in the substantia nigra, deep in the midbrain, go with slower reactions.

order.rationale: Volunteers were scanned once, two hours after the injection, and their mood and tiredness were asked about at two and three hours. The split into separate steps is a way of presenting those findings, not a measured sequence.

phases.name: Low mood, less pleasure
phases.timescale: two to three hours in the studies
phases.caption: Mood drops and things feel less rewarding. The more mood fell, the more active the subgenual cingulate was in that person, and the less it worked together with the amygdala, the medial prefrontal cortex and the nucleus accumbens. The ventral striatum responded less to the prospect of a reward.

order.rationale: The mood drop was significant at three hours, an hour after the scan. Placing it after the tiredness is a way of presenting the findings; the studies did not time the two against each other.

phases.name: Getting better
phases.caption: The infection clears and the sickness response fades. How the brain returns to normal was not studied in the sources read; this last part is an assumption.

order.rationale: No source read followed volunteers through recovery. The return to rest is assumed.

regions.explanation: Regions that represent the internal state of the body became more active under inflammation while volunteers did a demanding task, and their activity predicted how tired and foggy each person felt. They included the mid and front parts of the insula on both sides. A pooled analysis lists the insula among regions consistently affected by inflammation.

regions.explanation: The more a volunteer's mood fell after vaccination, the more active this region was while they looked at emotional faces. The region is one implicated in depression, and the authors take this to suggest a shared basis for low mood in illness and in depression. From one study of sixteen men. It is drawn at rest: the study found this only as a link with how far each person's mood fell, not as an average rise across everyone.

citations.quote: Inflammation-associated mood deterioration correlated with enhanced activity within subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sACC) (a region implicated in the etiology of depression) during emotional face processing.

citations.title: Inflammation causes mood changes through alterations in subgenual cingulate activity and mesolimbic connectivity.
citations.quote: The sACC activity reflected the interaction between processing of emotional facial expressions and inflammation-associated total mood change rather than as a main effect of processing emotional faces.

regions.explanation: Drawn on the nucleus accumbens, the main part of the ventral striatum. The finding is a weaker response to the prospect of a reward, not lower activity at rest. The ventral striatum responded less to signs of a coming reward in people given a mild immune challenge than in people given a placebo, and that weaker response accounted for part of their drop in mood. From one study of thirty-nine people. A pooled analysis also lists the striatum, mainly the caudate and putamen, among regions affected by inflammation, without regard to direction.
